Exact Recovery Thresholds for Weighted Data Selection
in Vector-Valued Linear RegressionThanks: The scalar case m=1m=1 of the problem is treated in our companion paper (Zhang, 2026), arXiv:2608.28007, by the same author.

Guangjian Zhang Affiliation: University of New South Wales Email: zgj1226029469@outlook.com
October 2, 2026
Abstract

We resolve the threshold part of Question 4 of the COLT 2025 open problem “Data Selection for Regression Tasks” of Hanneke, Moran, Shlimovich and Yehudayoff. We study vector-valued linear regression with square loss ℓ(x,y)​(W)=∥W​x−y∥22\ell_{(x,y)}(W)=\lVert Wx-y\rVert_{2}^{2}, where x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and y∈ℝmy\in\mathbb{R}^{m}. The learner returns the minimum-Frobenius-norm empirical risk minimizer. We prove that the minimal budget of weighted examples for recovering the full-data loss on every finite dataset is exactly n⋆​(d,m)=(m+1)​dn^{\star}(d,m)=(m+1)d. We determine the weighted selection profile Fweighted​(d,m,n)F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,n) at the near-threshold budget: Fweighted​(d,m,(m+1)​d−1)=1+1/(d​m2)F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,(m+1)d-1)=1+1/(dm^{2}). We recover the known spanning-budget value Fweighted​(d,m,d)=d+1F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,d)=d+1 for every mm, and Fweighted​(d,m,n)=∞F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,n)=\infty for n<dn<d. For the smallest open intermediate cell (d,m)=(2,2)(d,m)=(2,2) we prove Fweighted​(2,2,3)∈[13/8, 15/8]F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(2,2,3)\in[13/8,\,15/8] and Fweighted​(2,2,4)∈[5/4, 3/2]F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(2,2,4)\in[5/4,\,3/2]. We reduce the conjectured exact values 13/813/8 and 5/45/4 to a finite moment problem on the circle with at most seven atoms and assemble structural evidence for it. The upper bounds use a fixed-basis conic compression lemma, a determinant–facet rigidity theorem for maximal certificates, and sharp sparsification lemmas for zero-mean weighted point systems. These tools may be of independent interest. We also exhibit an explicit six-point integer dataset with d=m=2d=m=2 on which no weighted selection of 2​d2d points recovers the optimal loss. Thus the scalar sufficient budget 2​d2d does not extend to vector-valued outputs. Our new regression-profile results for m≥2m\geq 2 extend the scalar theory for m=1m=1.

1 Introduction

Data curation and reusable representations (Gadre et al., 2023; Oquab et al., 2023) call for precise theoretical benchmarks for data selection.

How well can a fixed, natural learning rule learn from only nn examples selected from a larger dataset? This question underlies coreset construction, data pruning and subsampling for regression. A typical multi-output instance is a linear head trained on a fixed representation, where all outputs must share one selected set of examples and one weight vector. Hanneke et al. (2025b) posed a worst-case version for basic regression in a COLT 2025 open-problem note, with a companion paper (Hanneke et al., 2025a). For scalar linear regression they determined the endpoint regimes under weighted selection and the minimum-norm empirical risk minimizer. The worst-case ratio between the selected model’s loss and the optimal full-data loss is infinite for n<dn<d, equals d+1d+1 at n=dn=d, and equals 11 for n≥2​dn\geq 2d (Hanneke et al., 2025b, Theorem 1). The intermediate range d<n<2​dd<n<2d was posed as their Question 2. Their note concludes with a unified vector-valued formulation using predictors W:ℝd→ℝmW\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{m}, square loss and the minimum Frobenius-norm ERM. It asks, as Question 4:

Given d,m,nd,m,n, what is the value of Fweighted​(d,m,n)F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,n)? In particular, what is the minimal n=n⁡(d,m)n=n(d,m) such that this ratio equals 11?

This paper resolves the threshold question completely and determines several further values of the profile Fweighted(d,m,⋅)F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,\cdot). Throughout, a dataset D=(zi)i=1ND=(z_{i})_{i=1}^{N} is a finite sequence of points zi=(xi,yi)∈ℝd×ℝmz_{i}=(x_{i},y_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{m}. We write ℓz​(W)=∥W​x−y∥22\ell_{z}(W)=\lVert Wx-y\rVert_{2}^{2}, LD​(W)=1N​∑iℓzi​(W)L_{D}(W)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\ell_{z_{i}}(W) and LD⋆=minW⁡LD​(W)L^{\star}_{D}=\min_{W}L_{D}(W). The learner AA returns the empirical risk minimizer of minimal Frobenius norm. Weighted selection of budget nn chooses nn points of DD (repetitions allowed) and a convex combination FF of their losses. Its loss on the full dataset is LD​(A​(F))L_{D}(A(F)). The profile Fweighted​(d,m,n)F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,n) is the supremum over datasets of infFLD​(A⁡(F))/LD⋆\inf_{F}L_{D}(A(F))/L^{\star}_{D}, with degenerate-ratio conventions fixed in Section 2. The exact-recovery threshold is n⋆​(d,m)=min⁡{n:Fweighted​(d,m,n)=1}n^{\star}(d,m)=\min\{n:F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,n)=1\}.

Contributions.

All statements below are for d,m≥2d,m\geq 2. They hold verbatim for d,m≥1d,m\geq 1 (Remark 2.4).

  • Exact threshold (Theorem 3.4): n⋆​(d,m)=(m+1)​dn^{\star}(d,m)=(m+1)d. The upper bound is data-dependent: every dataset of feature rank r≥1r\geq 1 is recovered exactly by (m+1)​r(m+1)r weighted points (Theorem 3.1). The lower bound is an explicit integer dataset on (m+1)​d(m+1)d points whose optimal ratio at budget (m+1)​d−1(m+1)d-1 is exactly 1+m+12​m​d​(m2+m−1)1+\frac{m+1}{2md(m^{2}+m-1)} (Theorem 3.3).

  • Near-threshold value (Theorem 5.2): Fweighted​(d,m,(m+1)​d−1)=1+1/(d​m2)F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,(m+1)d-1)=1+1/(dm^{2}). The proof hinges on rigidity of maximal exact certificates (Theorem 4.1). Every dataset unrecoverable within budget (m+1)​d−1(m+1)d-1 has a minimal spanning zero certificate whose support decomposes into dd disjoint (m+1)(m+1)-point residual circuits on independent feature lines. All nonzero features of such a dataset lie on these lines (Theorem 4.2). A sharp mm-point mean lemma (Lemma 5.1) then finishes the argument.

  • Low budgets (Theorem 6.1): Fweighted​(d,m,n)=∞F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,n)=\infty for n<dn<d and Fweighted​(d,m,d)=d+1F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,d)=d+1, independently of mm, as a direct consequence of Dereziński and Warmuth (2017) and the scalar lower bounds. A shared volume-sampling subset serves all output rows.

  • The smallest open cell (d,m)=(2,2)(d,m)=(2,2) (Section 6.2): Fweighted​(2,2,3)∈[13/8,15/8]F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(2,2,3)\in[13/8,15/8] and Fweighted​(2,2,4)∈[5/4,3/2]F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(2,2,4)\in[5/4,3/2] (Theorem 6.4). The conjectured values 13/813/8 and 5/45/4 are reduced to a finite-dimensional moment problem with at most seven atoms on the unit circle (Proposition 6.6). For this moment problem, we prove a sharp result for the two-direction class, stratified local maximality, two exact obstructions, and closure of several classes (Appendix F).

  • A byproduct: the scalar sufficient budget 2​d2d fails for every m≥2m\geq 2. On an explicit six-point integer dataset with d=m=2d=m=2, every weighted selection of four points has loss at least 2320​LD⋆\frac{23}{20}L^{\star}_{D} (Proposition 5.3).

Table 1 summarizes the resulting picture of the profile.

Techniques.

The threshold upper bound uses a fixed-basis conic compression lemma (Lemma B.1). After we pin a feature basis of rr points, the negated sum of their residual dyads lies in the cone of the remaining dyads. Conic Carathéodory represents it with at most m​rmr of them, giving an exact certificate on (m+1)​r(m+1)r points. The argument is shorter than the Steinitz-based scalar route of Hanneke et al. (2025a) and is data-dependent. The near-threshold upper bound uses a determinant–facet rigidity theorem (Theorem 4.1). Consider a certificate of maximal size (m+1)​d(m+1)d. Its weighted feature Gram determinant is a polynomial of degree at most dd in the weights, although the dyads span an m​dmd-dimensional space. It vanishes on every facet of the normalized certificate polytope. This forces a simplex and decomposes the certificate into dd disjoint (m+1)(m+1)-point circuits on dd independent feature lines. A sharp mm-point mean lemma for zero-mean weighted point systems then finishes the assembly. For the (2,2)(2,2) cell, a complex-variable dictionary turns whitened instances into moment systems on the unit circle and the selection cost into a convex combination of two-point interpolation coefficients (Lemma 6.2).

1.1 Related and concurrent work

Prior work. The problem and the scalar endpoint results are due to Hanneke et al. (2025b); Hanneke et al. (2025a). The scalar value at n=2​d−1n=2d-1 is proved in Dewasurendra (2026a) and Zhang (2026), and further scalar intermediate values in Zhang (2026). The budget-dd upper bound uses volume sampling and the exact expectation formulas of Dereziński and Warmuth (2017) (Theorem 5, used as an inequality; Section 6.1). The general kk-point mean lemma (Theorem G.1) is proved in Appendix G by an elementary argument. For k=2k=2 and M≥3M\geq 3, its constant coincides with, and follows from, Theorem 2 of Dewasurendra (2026b). That theorem covers neither M=2M=2 nor general kk. Tinarrage (2026) proves a radius-normalized, equal-weight analogue. Carathéodory-type compressions also underlie exact weighted coresets for least squares. For example, the summaries of Maalouf et al. (2019) preserve the covariance sums of the input. An exact coreset preserves the objective for every parameter. Here the summary must reproduce the model returned by a fixed learner retrained on the selected original points. We obtain matching lower bounds on the support and exact worst-case ratios below it.

Concurrent unrefereed preprints. Recent unrefereed preprints treat other questions of Hanneke et al. (2025b): Dewasurendra (2026b) determines the budget-22 column of Question 1, and Dewasurendra (2026a) proves the scalar value at budget 2​d−12d-1 (Question 2). Neither manuscript treats the weighted vector-valued Question 4. The relation of our sparsification results to Theorem 2 of Dewasurendra (2026b) is stated above. We make no priority claim on them.

Companion paper.

The scalar case m=1m=1, Question 2 of Hanneke et al. (2025b), is the subject of our companion paper (Zhang, 2026), available as arXiv:2608.28007. The two papers are by the same author.

Organization.

Sections 2–6 give results and proof sketches. Appendices A–F give full proofs. Appendix G gives the general kk-point mean lemma.

2 Recovery certificates and proof architecture

Throughout, d,m,n≥1d,m,n\geq 1 are integers. A dataset is a finite sequence D=(zi)i=1ND=(z_{i})_{i=1}^{N} of points zi=(xi,yi)∈ℝd×ℝmz_{i}=(x_{i},y_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{m}, N≥1N\geq 1, with repetitions allowed. A linear predictor W∈ℝm×dW\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} has loss ℓz​(W)=∥W​x−y∥22\ell_{z}(W)=\lVert Wx-y\rVert_{2}^{2} and average loss LD​(W)=1N​∑i=1Nℓzi​(W)L_{D}(W)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\ell_{z_{i}}(W). Write LD⋆=minW⁡LD​(W)L^{\star}_{D}=\min_{W}L_{D}(W). The learning rule AA maps a nonnegatively weighted objective F=∑ici​ℓziF=\sum_{i}c_{i}\ell_{z_{i}} (with ci≥0c_{i}\geq 0, ∑ici=1\sum_{i}c_{i}=1) to the minimum-Frobenius-norm minimizer of FF. For c∈ℝ≥0Nc\in\mathbb{R}^{N}_{\geq 0} write Fc=∑ici​ℓziF_{c}=\sum_{i}c_{i}\ell_{z_{i}}. Certificates below are nonzero and unnormalized. For such cc, we set A⁡(Fc):=A⁡(Fc/∑ici)A(F_{c}):=A(F_{c/\sum_{i}c_{i}}), the minimal-norm minimizer of FcF_{c} (positive rescaling preserves the minimizer set). The smallest full-data loss achievable by weighted selection with budget nn is

LD⋆​(n,weighted)=infzj1,…,zjn∈DF∈conv⁡(ℓzj1,…,ℓzjn)LD​(A⁡(F)),L^{\star}_{D}(n;\mathrm{weighted})=\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}z_{j_{1}},\dots,z_{j_{n}}\in D\\ F\in\operatorname{conv}(\ell_{z_{j_{1}}},\dots,\ell_{z_{j_{n}}})\end{subarray}}L_{D}\bigl(A(F)\bigr),
RD​(n)=LD⋆​(n,weighted)LD⋆,Fweighted​(d,m,n)=supDRD​(n),R_{D}(n)=\frac{L^{\star}_{D}(n;\mathrm{weighted})}{L^{\star}_{D}},\qquad F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,n)=\sup_{D}\,R_{D}(n),

where the supremum is over all datasets (all N≥1N\geq 1), and n⋆​(d,m)=min⁡{n:Fweighted​(d,m,n)=1}n^{\star}(d,m)=\min\{n:F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,n)=1\}. Following the convention of Hanneke et al. (2025a), RD​(n)R_{D}(n) is 11 when numerator and denominator are both 00, and ∞\infty when only the denominator is 00. Since LD​(A⁡(F))≥LD⋆L_{D}(A(F))\geq L^{\star}_{D} for every objective FF, RD​(n)≥1R_{D}(n)\geq 1. We write the inner optimization as an infimum (as in Hanneke et al. (2025a)): all exact-recovery certificates below are attained, while some bounds in Section 6.2 are limits of admissible selections. The following normalization is immediate and used implicitly.

Lemma 2.1 (Selection semantics).

Selections of budget nn are in value-preserving correspondence with weight vectors c∈ℝ≥0Nc\in\mathbb{R}^{N}_{\geq 0}, ∑ici=1\sum_{i}c_{i}=1, |supp⁡c|≤n|\operatorname{supp}c|\leq n. Repeated picks merge weights, and zero-weight picks can be discarded. Any cc with |supp⁡c|≤n|\operatorname{supp}c|\leq n is realizable with exactly nn slots by repeating a chosen point and splitting its weight. In particular the feasible family grows with nn, so LD⋆​(n,weighted)L^{\star}_{D}(n;\mathrm{weighted}), RD​(n)R_{D}(n) and Fweighted​(d,m,n)F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,n) are nonincreasing in nn.

Geometry of the full-data minimizer.

Let T=span⁡{x1,…,xN}T=\operatorname{span}\{x_{1},\dots,x_{N}\}, r=dimTr=\dim T (the feature rank), and let PTP_{T} be the orthogonal projection onto TT. Let W∘W^{\circ} be the minimal-Frobenius-norm full-data minimizer, and set ρi=W∘​xi−yi\rho_{i}=W^{\circ}x_{i}-y_{i} (residuals) and Mi=ρi​xi⊤∈ℝm×dM_{i}=\rho_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} (residual dyads). The objective and the squared Frobenius norm are additive across output rows, so A⁡(Fc)A(F_{c}) consists of the minimal-ℓ2\ell_{2}-norm scalar solutions row by row, with the single shared weight vector cc (Lemma A.1). Moreover, W∘=W∘​PTW^{\circ}=W^{\circ}P_{T}, the first-order condition ∑iMi=0\sum_{i}M_{i}=0 holds, and

LD​(W∘+H)=LD⋆+1N​∑i=1N∥H​xi∥2for every ​H∈ℝm×dL_{D}(W^{\circ}+H)=L^{\star}_{D}+\tfrac{1}{N}\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\lVert Hx_{i}\rVert^{2}\qquad\text{for every }H\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} (1)

(Lemma A.2). The two conditions in the next lemma have separate roles: the zero-dyad condition makes W∘W^{\circ} stationary for the selected objective, while the spanning condition makes the selected and full-data minimizer sets coincide.

Lemma 2.2 (Exact certificate).

Let c∈ℝ≥0Nc\in\mathbb{R}^{N}_{\geq 0} be nonzero, with support SS (so ci>0c_{i}>0 on SS). If

∑i∈Sci​Mi=0andspan⁡{xi:i∈S}=T,\sum_{i\in S}c_{i}M_{i}=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\operatorname{span}\{x_{i}:i\in S\}=T, (2)

then A⁡(Fc)=W∘A(F_{c})=W^{\circ}. In particular, the selection realizes the full-data optimal loss, and the ratio is 11 (also when LD⋆=0L^{\star}_{D}=0, by the 0/00/0 convention).

We call a nonzero weight vector satisfying (2) a spanning zero certificate, and define the minimal certificate size

τ(D)=min{|suppc|:cis a spanning zero certificate}.\tau(D)\;=\;\min\bigl\{|\operatorname{supp}c|:\ c\ \text{is a spanning zero certificate}\bigr\}. (3)

Certificates are built from positive circuits of the residual dyads.

Definition 2.3 (Positive circuit).

For a family of vectors (ai)i∈J(a_{i})_{i\in J}, a nonempty set C⊆JC\subseteq J is a positive circuit if there are coefficients λi>0\lambda_{i}>0 (i∈Ci\in C) with ∑i∈Cλi​ai=0\sum_{i\in C}\lambda_{i}a_{i}=0 and dimker⁡[ai]i∈C=1\dim\ker[a_{i}]_{i\in C}=1. Equivalently, the positive dependence is unique up to scaling and no proper subset of CC supports a nonzero nonnegative dependence. The positive circuits are exactly the supports of the extreme rays of the cone {λ≥0:∑iλi​ai=0}\{\lambda\geq 0:\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}a_{i}=0\}. Every nonzero point of this cone is a positive combination of extreme rays (conic Carathéodory). A singleton {i}\{i\} with ai=0a_{i}=0 is a positive circuit.

Finally, scalar instances embed: if all mm coordinates of every label agree, then every row of the vector problem is the same scalar problem, so Fweighted​(d,m,n)≥Fweightedsc​(d,n)F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,n)\geq F^{\mathrm{sc}}_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,n), the scalar weighted profile of Hanneke et al. (2025b) (Lemma A.3).

Remark 2.4 (Range of validity).

Nothing in the proofs of Theorems 3.4, 5.2 and 6.1 uses d≥2d\geq 2 or m≥2m\geq 2: they hold for all d,m≥1d,m\geq 1. At m=1m=1 they specialize to n⋆​(d,1)=2​dn^{\star}(d,1)=2d and Fweighted​(d,1,2​d−1)=1+1dF_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,1,2d-1)=1+\frac{1}{d}, matching Hanneke et al. (2025b, Theorem 1), Dewasurendra (2026a) and Zhang (2026). At d=1d=1 the whole profile is Corollary G.3. We state the theorems for d,m≥2d,m\geq 2 only to delineate the new contribution: for m=1m=1 both conclusions of Theorem 6.1 and the threshold 2​d2d are due to Hanneke et al. (2025b); Hanneke et al. (2025a), and the value at n=2​d−1n=2d-1, stated in Hanneke et al. (2025b), is proved in Dewasurendra (2026a) and Zhang (2026). Our new regression-profile results concern the vector case m≥2m\geq 2.

Proof routes.

Selected reading links: Threshold: Lemmas A.2, 2.2, B.1; Theorems 3.1, 3.3, 3.4 (Appendices A–B). Near threshold: Definition 2.3; Theorems 4.1, 4.2; Lemma 5.1; Theorem 5.2 (Appendix D).

3 The exact threshold (m+1)​d(m+1)d

Upper bound: fixed-basis conic compression.

The key combinatorial fact is that a zero-sum family of vectors admits a nonnegative zero-sum subfamily that contains any prescribed index set BB and at most dimspan⁡{ai:i∉B}\dim\operatorname{span}\{a_{i}:i\notin B\} further elements (Lemma B.1, a consequence of conic Carathéodory). Applied to the residual dyads with BB a feature basis, it gives:

Theorem 3.1 (Data-dependent upper bound).

Every dataset with feature rank r≥1r\geq 1 admits a spanning zero certificate of support at most (m+1)​r(m+1)r. Hence τ⁡(D)≤(m+1)​r\tau(D)\leq(m+1)r and LD⋆​((m+1)​d,weighted)=LD⋆L^{\star}_{D}\bigl((m+1)d;\mathrm{weighted}\bigr)=L^{\star}_{D} for every dataset. If r=0r=0, a single point suffices.

Proof sketch.

Pick a basis BB of rr features. The dyads Mi=ρi​xi⊤M_{i}=\rho_{i}x_{i}^{\top} have all rows in TT, so the dyads outside BB span a space of dimension at most m​rmr. Lemma B.1 therefore yields c≥0c\geq 0, positive on BB, with ∑ici​Mi=0\sum_{i}c_{i}M_{i}=0 and support at most r+m​rr+mr. The support contains the basis, hence spans TT, and Lemma 2.2 gives A⁡(Fc)=W∘A(F_{c})=W^{\circ}. The full proof is in Appendix B. The same argument with s=dimspan⁡{ρi}s=\dim\operatorname{span}\{\rho_{i}\} replacing mm gives τ⁡(D)≤(s+1)​r\tau(D)\leq(s+1)r for r≥1r\geq 1 (Remark B.2): the dataset’s budget is governed by its effective residual output dimension. ∎

Lower bound: the axial simplex instance.

Fix d,m≥1d,m\geq 1, let 𝟏m\mathbf{1}_{m} be the all-ones vector, and let vj=ejv_{j}=e_{j} (1≤j≤m1\leq j\leq m), vm+1=−𝟏mv_{m+1}=-\mathbf{1}_{m}, so that ∑jvj=0\sum_{j}v_{j}=0 and no proper subset of {vj}\{v_{j}\} contains 00 in its convex hull.

Definition 3.2 (Integer axial instance).

Dd,mD_{d,m} consists of the N=(m+1)​dN=(m+1)d points zi​j=(ei, 1m−vj)z_{ij}=(e_{i},\,\mathbf{1}_{m}-v_{j}) for i∈[d]i\in[d], j∈[m+1]j\in[m+1]. Explicitly, the label of zi​jz_{ij} is 𝟏m−ej\mathbf{1}_{m}-e_{j} for j≤mj\leq m and 2⋅𝟏m2\cdot\mathbf{1}_{m} for j=m+1j=m+1.

On Dd,mD_{d,m} the unique full-data minimizer is W∘=𝟏m​𝟏d⊤W^{\circ}=\mathbf{1}_{m}\mathbf{1}_{d}^{\top} with residual vjv_{j} at zi​jz_{ij} and LD⋆=2​mm+1L^{\star}_{D}=\frac{2m}{m+1}. The weighted normal equations decouple across the dd axes. The returned column on an axis is the conditional weighted mean of its labels (or 00 if the axis is unused). The returned model’s loss exceeds LD⋆L^{\star}_{D} by 1d​∑i∥δi∥2\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i}\lVert\delta_{i}\rVert^{2}, where δi\delta_{i} is the deviation of column ii from 𝟏m\mathbf{1}_{m} (Lemma B.3). With Qm=m2+m−1Q_{m}=m^{2}+m-1, the squared distance from the origin to the convex hull of any nonempty proper subset of {vj}\{v_{j}\} is at least 1/Qm1/Q_{m}, attained on the facets omitting some eke_{k} (Lemma B.4).

Theorem 3.3 (Exact deficit of the axial instance).

For every d,m≥1d,m\geq 1,

LDd,m⋆​((m+1)​d−1,weighted)LDd,m⋆= 1+m+12​m​d​(m2+m−1)> 1.\frac{L^{\star}_{D_{d,m}}\bigl((m+1)d-1;\mathrm{weighted}\bigr)}{L^{\star}_{D_{d,m}}}\;=\;1+\frac{m+1}{2md\,(m^{2}+m-1)}\;>\;1.
Proof sketch.

A selection of support at most N−1N-1 leaves some axis either empty (deviation ∥𝟏m∥2=m\lVert\mathbf{1}_{m}\rVert^{2}=m) or supported on a proper subset of its m+1m+1 points (deviation at least 1/Qm1/Q_{m} by Lemma B.4), so the excess loss is at least 1d​Qm\frac{1}{dQ_{m}}. Omitting one point e1e_{1} on one axis and using the facet-foot weights there attains this bound. Dividing by LD⋆L^{\star}_{D} gives the value. ∎

Theorem 3.4 (Threshold).

n⋆​(d,m)=(m+1)​dn^{\star}(d,m)=(m+1)d for all d,m≥2d,m\geq 2 (and in fact for all d,m≥1d,m\geq 1, cf. Remark 2.4), and Fweighted​(d,m,n)=1F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,n)=1 for all n≥(m+1)​dn\geq(m+1)d.

Proof.

Theorem 3.1 gives ratio 11 at budget (m+1)​d(m+1)d for every dataset. Theorem 3.3 exhibits a dataset with ratio >1>1 at budget (m+1)​d−1(m+1)d-1, and Fweighted(d,m,⋅)F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,\cdot) is nonincreasing (Lemma 2.1). ∎

Corollary 3.5.

n⋆​(2,2)=6n^{\star}(2,2)=6. On the instance D2,2D_{2,2} (six integer points, labels (0,1),(1,0),(2,2)(0,1),(1,0),(2,2) over each of e1,e2e_{1},e_{2}) the optimal five-point ratio is exactly 4340\tfrac{43}{40}.

4 Rigidity of maximal certificates

Theorem 3.1 gives τ⁡(D)≤max⁡{1,(m+1)​r}\tau(D)\leq\max\{1,(m+1)r\}. The upper bound at budget (m+1)​d−1(m+1)d-1 requires understanding the datasets with τ⁡(D)=(m+1)​d\tau(D)=(m+1)d, which we call certificate-maximal. The key is a rigidity theorem for maximal certificates.

Theorem 4.1 (Determinant–facet rigidity).

Let the features span ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and suppose τ⁡(D)=k:=(m+1)​d\tau(D)=k:=(m+1)d. Let cc be a spanning zero certificate with |supp⁡c|=k|\operatorname{supp}c|=k and support SS. Then SS splits uniquely (up to permutation) into dd pairwise disjoint blocks S=C1⊔⋯⊔CdS=C_{1}\sqcup\dots\sqcup C_{d} with |Cj|=m+1|C_{j}|=m+1, where each CjC_{j} supports a positive circuit of the dyads whose features span a one-dimensional line UjU_{j}, and U1,…,UdU_{1},\dots,U_{d} are linearly independent.

Proof sketch.

Vectorize the dyads of SS into a matrix 𝖠\mathsf{A} with m​dmd rows and kk columns. The normalized nonnegative kernel P={θ≥0:𝖠θ=0, 1⊤θ=1}P=\{\theta\geq 0:\mathsf{A}\theta=0,\ \mathbf{1}^{\top}\theta=1\} is a polytope of dimension h−1≥d−1h-1\geq d-1 whose relative interior consists of the strictly positive points. The polynomial f⁡(θ)=det(∑iθi​xi​xi⊤)f(\theta)=\det(\sum_{i}\theta_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}), of degree at most dd, is positive on the relative interior and must vanish at every boundary point: a boundary point with f>0f>0 would be a spanning zero certificate of smaller support. A nonzero polynomial of degree ≤d\leq d vanishing on every facet is divisible by the facets’ affine forms, so PP has at most dd facets. A bounded (h−1)(h-1)-polytope has at least hh facets, so h=dh=d and PP is a simplex (a point if d=1d=1). The dd extreme rays give the blocks CjC_{j}. Dropping a ray gives a boundary point where the features cannot span. This forces the feature spans UjU_{j} of the blocks to be a minimal spanning family, hence lines. The bound |Cj|≤m+1|C_{j}|\leq m+1 then forces |Cj|=m+1|C_{j}|=m+1 and disjointness. The full proof is in Appendix D. ∎

Using the maximality of τ⁡(D)\tau(D) once more, the same line-circuit structure governs every nonzero-feature point:

Theorem 4.2 (Line structure).

Let the features span ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and τ⁡(D)=(m+1)​d=k\tau(D)=(m+1)d=k. Then:

  1. 1.

    every data point with xi≠0x_{i}\neq 0 belongs to some positive circuit of dyads supported on a single feature line and of size exactly m+1m+1;

  2. 2.

    there is no positive circuit of dyads whose features span a subspace of dimension ≥2\geq 2, and no line circuit of size ≤m\leq m; in particular no point has xi≠0x_{i}\neq 0 and ρi=0\rho_{i}=0;

  3. 3.

    the nonzero features lie on exactly dd linearly independent lines.

Consequently, any dataset whose nonzero features are not of this dd-line form satisfies τ⁡(D)≤(m+1)​d−1\tau(D)\leq(m+1)d-1 and is recovered exactly within budget (m+1)​d−1(m+1)d-1.

5 The near-threshold value 1+1/(d​m2)1+1/(dm^{2})

The assembly needs one more ingredient: a sharp sparsification bound for zero-mean weighted point systems. The general kk-point version is Theorem G.1. The case below is elementary:

Lemma 5.1 (mm-point mean lemma).

Let zi∈ℝmz_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} carry weights pi>0p_{i}>0 with ∑ipi=1\sum_{i}p_{i}=1 and ∑ipi​zi=0\sum_{i}p_{i}z_{i}=0, and let E=∑ipi​∥zi∥2E=\sum_{i}p_{i}\lVert z_{i}\rVert^{2}. Then some convex combination δ\delta of at most mm of the points satisfies ∥δ∥2≤E/m2\lVert\delta\rVert^{2}\leq E/m^{2}. The constant is attained by the uniformly weighted regular simplex.

Proof sketch.

Decompose pp into positive circuits and choose one with second moment at most EE. For a circuit q1,…,qm+1>0q_{1},\dots,q_{m+1}>0, deleting point jj leaves the mm-point mean μj=−qj1−qj​zj\mu_{j}=-\frac{q_{j}}{1-q_{j}}z_{j}. The inequality ∑j(1−qj)2/qj≥m2\sum_{j}(1-q_{j})^{2}/q_{j}\geq m^{2} (Cauchy–Schwarz) shows that not all jj can violate ∥μj∥2≤E/m2\lVert\mu_{j}\rVert^{2}\leq E/m^{2}. The full proof is in Appendix D. ∎

Theorem 5.2 (Near-threshold value).

For all d,m≥2d,m\geq 2 (and in fact for all d,m≥1d,m\geq 1, cf. Remark 2.4), Fweighted​(d,m,(m+1)​d−1)=1+1d​m2F_{\mathrm{weighted}}\bigl(d,m,(m+1)d-1\bigr)=1+\dfrac{1}{dm^{2}}.

Proof sketch.

Upper bound. If the feature rank is below dd, or LD⋆=0L^{\star}_{D}=0, or τ⁡(D)≤(m+1)​d−1\tau(D)\leq(m+1)d-1, the ratio is 11. Otherwise Theorem 4.2 places all nonzero features on dd independent lines u1,…,udu_{1},\dots,u_{d}, with xi=si​uj⁡(i)x_{i}=s_{i}u_{j(i)}. The first-order condition splits into one zero-mean condition per line, ∑i∈Ijsi​ρi=0\sum_{i\in I_{j}}s_{i}\rho_{i}=0. Let zi=ρi/siz_{i}=\rho_{i}/s_{i} and pi=si2/∑Ijsi′2p_{i}=s_{i}^{2}/\sum_{I_{j}}s_{i^{\prime}}^{2}, so that ∑Ijpi​zi=0\sum_{I_{j}}p_{i}z_{i}=0 and ∑Ijpi​∥zi∥2=Rj/gj\sum_{I_{j}}p_{i}\lVert z_{i}\rVert^{2}=R_{j}/g_{j} with Rj=∑Ij∥ρi∥2R_{j}=\sum_{I_{j}}\lVert\rho_{i}\rVert^{2} and gj=∑Ijsi2g_{j}=\sum_{I_{j}}s_{i}^{2}. Choose the lightest line j⋆j_{\star} (Rj⋆≤N​LD⋆/dR_{j_{\star}}\leq NL^{\star}_{D}/d). Fit every other line exactly with a positive (m+1)(m+1)-point circuit, and line j⋆j_{\star} with the mm-point mean δ\delta of Lemma 5.1. The weighted normal equations decouple along the basis, giving W^=W∘+H\widehat{W}=W^{\circ}+H with H​uj=0Hu_{j}=0 for j≠j⋆j\neq j_{\star} and H​uj⋆=−δHu_{j_{\star}}=-\delta. By (1), the excess loss is gj⋆​∥δ∥2/N≤Rj⋆/(N​m2)≤LD⋆/(d​m2)g_{j_{\star}}\lVert\delta\rVert^{2}/N\leq R_{j_{\star}}/(Nm^{2})\leq L^{\star}_{D}/(dm^{2}) on a support of size (d−1)​(m+1)+m=(m+1)​d−1(d-1)(m+1)+m=(m+1)d-1. Lower bound. Take dd axes, each carrying the vertices w+rjw+r_{j} of a regular simplex r1,…,rm+1r_{1},\dots,r_{m+1} with ∥rj∥2=mm+1\lVert r_{j}\rVert^{2}=\frac{m}{m+1}. The simplex’s facets are at squared distance h2=1m⁡(m+1)h^{2}=\frac{1}{m(m+1)} from the origin, and we take ∥w∥=h\lVert w\rVert=h. Any selection of N−1N-1 points leaves an axis empty or on a proper subset, costing at least h2/dh^{2}/d in excess loss. Deleting one vertex attains this bound. The ratio is 1+h2/dm/(m+1)=1+1d​m21+\frac{h^{2}/d}{m/(m+1)}=1+\frac{1}{dm^{2}}. ∎

Failure at n=2​dn=2d for m≥2m\geq 2.

The scalar rule “n≥2​dn\geq 2d suffices” does not extend to vector outputs (Remark 5.4).

Proposition 5.3.

For all d≥1,m≥2d\geq 1,m\geq 2, Fweighted​(d,m,2​d)≥Fweighted​(d,m,(m+1)​d−1)= 1+1d​m2>1F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,2d)\ \geq\ F_{\mathrm{weighted}}\bigl(d,m,(m+1)d-1\bigr)\;=\;1+\frac{1}{dm^{2}}>1, since 2​d≤(m+1)​d−12d\leq(m+1)d-1 and FweightedF_{\mathrm{weighted}} is nonincreasing in nn. Concretely, for d=m=2d=m=2 the instance D2,2D_{2,2} of Corollary 3.5 satisfies: every weighted selection of at most 2​d=42d=4 points has

LD​(A⁡(F))≥2320⋅LD⋆,L_{D}(A(F))\;\geq\;\frac{23}{20}\cdot L^{\star}_{D},

with equality attained (allocate two points per axis, at conditional weights realizing the nearest facet points).

The proof enumerates per-axis costs and allocations (Appendix B).

Remark 5.4 (Scalar and vector recovery budgets).

The weighted scalar trichotomy of Hanneke et al. (2025b, Theorem 1) gives ratio 11 for all n≥2​dn\geq 2d. This sufficient budget does not extend to general mm: the scalar result applies to m=1m=1, whereas for every m≥2m\geq 2, Theorem 3.4 shows that worst-case exact recovery requires (m+1)​d>2​d(m+1)d>2d points. Quantitatively, Fweighted​(d,m,2​d)≥Fweighted​(d,m,(m+1)​d−1)=1+1d​m2>1F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,2d)\geq F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,(m+1)d-1)=1+\frac{1}{dm^{2}}>1 by monotonicity. Proposition 5.3 makes the failure concrete.

6 Further results on the selection profile

6.1 Low budgets n≤dn\leq d

Theorem 6.1.

For all d,m≥2d,m\geq 2 (and in fact for all d,m≥1d,m\geq 1, cf. Remark 2.4),

Fweighted​(d,m,n)=∞​ for every ​n<d,andFweighted​(d,m,d)=d+1.F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,n)=\infty\ \text{ for every }n<d,\qquad\text{and}\qquad F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,d)=d+1.

The lower bounds are inherited from the scalar case through Lemma A.3: by Hanneke et al. (2025b, Theorem 1), Fweightedsc​(d,n)=∞F^{\mathrm{sc}}_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,n)=\infty for n<dn<d and Fweightedsc​(d,d)=d+1F^{\mathrm{sc}}_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,d)=d+1. The content of the theorem is the upper bound Fweighted​(d,m,d)≤d+1F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,d)\leq d+1 uniformly in mm, which requires one subset serving all mm output rows simultaneously.

Proof sketch.

Let X∈ℝd×NX\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N} have full row rank and y∈ℝNy\in\mathbb{R}^{N}. Size-dd volume sampling draws dd columns with probability proportional to det(XS)2\det(X_{S})^{2}, and w⁡(S)w(S) is the interpolant of the subproblem. Dereziński and Warmuth (2017) proved that 𝔼⁡[L⁡(w⁡(S))]≤(d+1)​L​(w⋆)\mathbb{E}[L(w(S))]\leq(d+1)L(w^{\star}) for the total square loss, with equality when XX is in general position (their Theorem 5). We use only the inequality, which holds without general position. Equality can fail for degenerate XX; see Appendix C. The distribution over subsets depends only on the features. For a dataset of feature rank rr (the cases r=0r=0 and LD⋆=0L^{\star}_{D}=0 are trivial), we run size-rr volume sampling in coordinates of TT, apply the inequality to each of the mm output rows, and sum: 𝔼⁡[LD​(WS)]≤(r+1)​LD⋆≤(d+1)​LD⋆\mathbb{E}[L_{D}(W_{S})]\leq(r+1)L^{\star}_{D}\leq(d+1)L^{\star}_{D} for the matrix WSW_{S} whose rows are the per-row interpolants. Some subset SS achieves the bound, and WSW_{S} is exactly what the Frobenius rule returns on SS with any positive weights, since the rr selected features are linearly independent. ∎

6.2 The smallest intermediate cell (d,m)=(2,2)(d,m)=(2,2)

For d,m≥2d,m\geq 2 and d<n<(m+1)​d−1d<n<(m+1)d-1 the profile remains open (for d=1d=1 it is given by Corollary G.3). Apart from the cells settled by Zhang (2026), its scalar counterpart also remains open. We treat the smallest cell (d,m)=(2,2)(d,m)=(2,2), where the open budgets are n=3,4n=3,4.

A complex dictionary for the hard branches.

Fix a (2,2)(2,2) dataset of feature rank 22 with LD⋆>0L^{\star}_{D}>0 and τ⁡(D)>n\tau(D)>n. For selections whose features span ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, the weighted minimizer is unique. pi=|ξi|2∑j|ξj|2,ti=ξ¯iξi∈S1,zi=ηiξi∈ℂ,E=∑ipi​|zi|2>0.p_{i}=\frac{|\xi_{i}|^{2}}{\sum_{j}|\xi_{j}|^{2}},\qquad t_{i}=\frac{\bar{\xi}_{i}}{\xi_{i}}\in S^{1},\qquad z_{i}=\frac{\eta_{i}}{\xi_{i}}\in\mathbb{C},\qquad E=\sum_{i}p_{i}|z_{i}|^{2}>0.

With μ=𝔼q​t\mu=\mathbb{E}_{q}t, ν=𝔼q​z\nu=\mathbb{E}_{q}z, λ=𝔼q​(t¯​z)\lambda=\mathbb{E}_{q}(\bar{t}z), the map W∘−W^W^{\circ}-\widehat{W} is ξ↦a​ξ+b​ξ¯\xi\mapsto a\xi+b\bar{\xi} where

and the excess ratio of the selection is at most C⁡(q)/EC(q)/E with C⁡(q)=|a|2+|b|2C(q)=|a|^{2}+|b|^{2} (with equality when no feature vanishes; Appendix E.2). Lemma 6.2 (Interpolation convex combination).

Lower bounds.

Proposition 6.3.

There is an explicit dataset D△D^{\triangle} with

Theorem 6.4.

Fweighted​(2,2,3)∈[138,158]F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(2,2,3)\in\bigl[\frac{13}{8},\frac{15}{8}\bigr] and Fweighted​(2,2,4)∈[54,32]F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(2,2,4)\in\bigl[\frac{5}{4},\frac{3}{2}\bigr].

Proof sketch.

The lower bounds follow from Proposition 6.3. For the upper bounds, the branches of feature rank ≤1\leq 1, LD⋆=0L^{\star}_{D}=0, or τ⁡(D)≤n\tau(D)\leq n have ratio 11 (Theorem 3.1). Otherwise, the dictionary applies and the ratio is at most 1+Γ3≤1581+\Gamma_{3}\leq\frac{15}{8} for n=3n=3 and 1+Γ4≤321+\Gamma_{4}\leq\frac{3}{2} for n=4n=4. The closure points are limits of admissible selections within the same budget. This suffices for the inner infimum. The full proofs are in Appendix E. ∎

The conjecture and its reduction.

Conjecture 6.5.

Fweighted​(2,2,3)=138F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(2,2,3)=\frac{13}{8} and Fweighted​(2,2,4)=54F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(2,2,4)=\frac{5}{4}. Equivalently, for every moment system,

inf|supp⁡q|≤3,|μ|<1C⁡(q)≤5​E8andinf|supp⁡q|≤4,|μ|<1C⁡(q)≤E4.\inf_{|\operatorname{supp}q|\leq 3,\ |\mu|<1}C(q)\leq\frac{5E}{8}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\inf_{|\operatorname{supp}q|\leq 4,\ |\mu|<1}C(q)\leq\frac{E}{4}.

The two formulations are equivalent (Remark E.6), and the conjecture is a finite-dimensional problem:

Proposition 6.6.

For fixed atoms (ti,zi)(t_{i},z_{i}), the closed set 𝒫={p∈ℝ≥0N:∑ipi=1,𝔼pt=𝔼pz=𝔼p(t¯z)=0}\mathcal{P}=\{p\in\mathbb{R}^{N}_{\geq 0}:\sum_{i}p_{i}=1,\ \mathbb{E}_{p}t=\mathbb{E}_{p}z=\mathbb{E}_{p}(\bar{t}z)=0\} is a polytope cut out by at most 77 linear equalities. Its points with full support are the admissible weight vectors. Minimizing the linear functional E⁡(p)E(p) over this polytope yields a basic feasible solution p⋆p^{\star} of support at most 77 with E⁡(p⋆)≤E⁡(p)E(p^{\star})\leq E(p). The subsystem on supp⁡p⋆\operatorname{supp}p^{\star} is again a moment system, and every selection admissible for it is admissible for the original system. Consequently each inequality of Conjecture 6.5 holds for all finite systems if and only if it holds for all systems with at most seven atoms. Since atoms may be split into identically placed copies without changing anything, it suffices to treat systems with exactly seven labelled atoms.

Evidence.

Appendix F proves four further statements. (i) Two-direction systems (all atoms on two antipodal directions) satisfy both conjectured inequalities. Both constants are attained simultaneously by six equally weighted atoms forming an equilateral zz-triangle over each direction. For the three-point bound, this is, up to merging coincident atoms, the only equality configuration (Proposition F.1). (ii) The equality fiber is a stratified local maximum of the normalized three-point value E−1​infCE^{-1}\inf C: energy imbalance gives the cusp 18​(5−3​|η|)\frac{1}{8}(5-3|\eta|) below its value 58\frac{5}{8}, and splitting a direction class drops it to lim sup≤12\limsup\leq\frac{1}{2} (Proposition F.2). (iii) Two exact obstructions: a proof cannot restrict to selections with μ=0\mu=0 (for the seventh-roots system tj=ζjt_{j}=\zeta^{j}, zj=ζ3​jz_{j}=\zeta^{3j}, Parseval forces C≥38,23C\geq\frac{3}{8},\frac{2}{3} at supports 4,34,3, while unconstrained selections reach <14<\frac{1}{4} and 27\frac{2}{7}). It also cannot rest on comparing aggregate second moments of original-weight subsets (for the fifth-roots system the aggregate quotient is 1523>58\frac{15}{23}>\frac{5}{8}) (Propositions F.3–F.4). (iv) Closed classes:

Proposition 6.7 (Classes on which Conjecture 6.5 holds).

The three-point inequality of Conjecture 6.5 holds for all moment systems with at most four atoms. The four-point inequality holds for all systems with at most five atoms. Both inequalities hold for all two-direction systems, and the four-point inequality holds for all antipodally paired systems (disjoint unions of pairs {(t,z),(−t,z)}\{(t,z),(-t,z)\} with equal zz-values inside each pair).

Moreover, by Lemma E.4 any counterexample to the three-point inequality must satisfy 5​|zi|2−2​Li>3​E5|z_{i}|^{2}-2L_{i}>3E for every atom. The regular hexagon third-harmonic system has three-point value exactly 12\frac{1}{2} and four-point value 00.

7 Discussion and open problems

The threshold splits conceptually as (m+1)​d=d+m​d(m+1)d=d+md: dd points to pin a feature basis and m​dmd points to cancel the m×dm\times d residual gradient. The lower-bound instances realize this as dd independent copies of weighted mean estimation in ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m}, one per feature direction. Each requires its full simplex of m+1m+1 points. At m=1m=1 the two mechanisms coincide. Table 2 in Appendix E separates the values of explicit instances from the global profile values at (2,2)(2,2). Our theorems concern a fixed learner and a fixed finite dataset. Certificates use the full-data minimizer W∘W^{\circ}, with arbitrary nonnegative real weights. Some intermediate bounds are attained only as limits. The theorems describe what a small weighted subsample can represent and its exact budget limits. They provide neither a faster selection algorithm nor guarantees for unseen data.

Open problems.

(1) The intermediate curve. Determine Fweighted​(d,m,n)F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,n) for d,m≥2d,m\geq 2 and d<n<(m+1)​d−1d<n<(m+1)d-1. Even the scalar case is largely open (Hanneke et al. (2025b), Question 2; see Zhang (2026) for the cells resolved so far). Axial instances reduce to an allocation problem over per-line mean-estimation deficits (Theorem G.1 supplies the sharp per-line constants). (2) The (2,2)(2,2) cell (Conjecture 6.5): a question about at most seven atoms on the circle. A proof must use selections with μ≠0\mu\neq 0 and cannot rest on comparing aggregate second moments of original-weight subsets. (3) Unweighted vector selection. Relating the unweighted profile F⁡(d,m,n)F(d,m,n) of Question 3 of Hanneke et al. (2025b) to the weighted threshold (m+1)​d(m+1)d. (4) Other learning rules. How does the threshold depend on the ERM tie-breaking rule? Our upper bounds use it only through Lemma 2.2, while the lower bounds use it in their rank-deficient branches.

7.1 Conclusion

We establish the exact threshold n⋆​(d,m)=(m+1)​dn^{\star}(d,m)=(m+1)d for weighted data selection with the minimum-Frobenius-norm ERM to recover the full-data loss of every dataset. This answers the threshold part of Question 4 posed at COLT 2025 by Hanneke et al. (2025b). We also determine the profile at two further budgets, Fweighted​(d,m,(m+1)​d−1)=1+1/(d​m2)F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,(m+1)d-1)=1+1/(dm^{2}) and Fweighted​(d,m,d)=d+1F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,d)=d+1. The proofs rest on three reusable tools: fixed-basis conic compression, determinant–facet rigidity of maximal certificates, and sharp sparsification of zero-mean weighted point systems. The proofs also use a complex-variable dictionary that reduces the smallest open cell to a seven-atom moment problem. The intermediate curve d<n<(m+1)​d−1d<n<(m+1)d-1 for d,m≥2d,m\geq 2 remains open. For d=1d=1 the complete curve is given by Corollary G.3. Even on the open curve the inner infimum in FweightedF_{\mathrm{weighted}} need not be attained (Remark E.2: an integer instance with d=m=2d=m=2, n=3n=3). The first target is the (2,2)(2,2) conjecture Fweighted​(2,2,3)=13/8F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(2,2,3)=13/8, Fweighted​(2,2,4)=5/4F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(2,2,4)=5/4.

Proofs and exact verification

All results are mathematical. Complete proofs of every theorem, lemma and proposition of Sections 2–6.2 are given in Appendices A–F. The general sparsification theorem is proved in Appendix G. Conjecture 6.5 remains open. Appendix F provides partial results and evidence for it. The explicit instances in Definition 3.2 and Proposition 6.3, along with the moment systems of Appendix F, are given in closed form with rational or algebraic coordinates. Every numerical value in the paper can therefore be recomputed by exact arithmetic from the formulas in the text. These include 43/4043/40, 23/2023/20, 13/813/8, 5/45/4, 1/21/2, 4/74/7, 2/72/7, 15/2315/23, the hexagon four-point value 00, and the constants of Lemma 5.1 and Theorem G.1. We performed these exact computations as a supplementary check. No numerical search is used in the proof of any theorem.

This appendix proves the structural lemmas of Section 2.

A.1 Row decomposition and minimum-norm geometry

Lemma A.1 (Row decomposition).

Write wj⊤w_{j}^{\top} for the jj-th row of WW and yi​jy_{ij} for the jj-th entry of yiy_{i}. Then Fc​(W)=∑j=1m∑ici​(⟨wj,xi⟩−yi​j)2F_{c}(W)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sum_{i}c_{i}(\langle w_{j},x_{i}\rangle-y_{ij})^{2} and ∥W∥F2=∑j∥wj∥2\lVert W\rVert_{F}^{2}=\sum_{j}\lVert w_{j}\rVert^{2}. Hence the minimizer set of FcF_{c} is the Cartesian product over rows of scalar weighted least-squares solution sets. The model A⁡(Fc)A(F_{c}) consists of the minimal-ℓ2\ell_{2}-norm scalar solutions row by row, with the single shared weight vector cc.

Proof.

Both the objective and the squared Frobenius norm are additive across rows, and a product set is minimized in norm coordinate-wise. ∎

Let T=span⁡{x1,…,xN}T=\operatorname{span}\{x_{1},\dots,x_{N}\}, r=dimTr=\dim T, and let PTP_{T} denote the orthogonal projection onto TT. Let W∘W^{\circ} be the minimal-Frobenius-norm full-data minimizer, and set ρi=W∘​xi−yi\rho_{i}=W^{\circ}x_{i}-y_{i} (residuals) and Mi=ρi​xi⊤∈ℝm×dM_{i}=\rho_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} (residual dyads).

Lemma A.2 (Full-data geometry).

W∘=W∘​PTW^{\circ}=W^{\circ}P_{T}. The first-order condition ∑i=1NMi=0\sum_{i=1}^{N}M_{i}=0 holds, and for every H∈ℝm×dH\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d},

LD​(W∘+H)=LD⋆+1N​∑i=1N∥H​xi∥2.L_{D}(W^{\circ}+H)=L^{\star}_{D}+\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\lVert Hx_{i}\rVert^{2}. (5)

Consequently, the full-data minimizer set is {W∘+H:H​PT=0}\{W^{\circ}+H:HP_{T}=0\}. If T=ℝdT=\mathbb{R}^{d}, the minimizer is unique.

Proof.

Predictions depend on WW only through W​PTWP_{T}, and ∥W∥F2=∥W​PT∥F2+∥W​PT⟂∥F2\lVert W\rVert_{F}^{2}=\lVert WP_{T}\rVert_{F}^{2}+\lVert WP_{T^{\perp}}\rVert_{F}^{2}, so minimality of the norm forces W∘​PT⟂=0W^{\circ}P_{T^{\perp}}=0. Expanding LD​(W∘+H)L_{D}(W^{\circ}+H), the cross term is 2N​⟨H,∑iMi⟩F=0\frac{2}{N}\langle H,\sum_{i}M_{i}\rangle_{F}=0, giving (5). The excess term in (5) vanishes iff H​xi=0Hx_{i}=0 for all ii, i.e. H​PT=0HP_{T}=0, which identifies the minimizer set. ∎

The two conditions in the next lemma have separate roles: the zero-dyad condition makes W∘W^{\circ} stationary for the selected objective, while the spanning condition makes the selected and full-data minimizer sets coincide.

Lemma 2.2 (Exact certificate; restated). Let c∈ℝ≥0Nc\in\mathbb{R}^{N}_{\geq 0} be nonzero, with support SS (so ci>0c_{i}>0 on SS). If

∑i∈Sci​Mi=0andspan⁡{xi:i∈S}=T,\sum_{i\in S}c_{i}M_{i}=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\operatorname{span}\{x_{i}:i\in S\}=T,

B.1 Upper bound: fixed-basis conic compression

Lemma B.1 (Fixed-basis conic compression).

Let a1,…,aNa_{1},\dots,a_{N} be elements of a finite-dimensional real vector space with ∑i=1Nai=0\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{i}=0, and let B⊆[N]B\subseteq[N]. Put qB=dimspan⁡{ai:i∉B}q_{B}=\dim\operatorname{span}\{a_{i}:i\notin B\}. Then there exist coefficients ci≥0c_{i}\geq 0 with cb>0c_{b}>0 for all b∈Bb\in B, ∑ici​ai=0\sum_{i}c_{i}a_{i}=0, and |supp⁡c|≤|B|+qB|\operatorname{supp}c|\leq|B|+q_{B}.

Proof.

The global zero sum gives −∑b∈Bab=∑i∉Bai-\sum_{b\in B}a_{b}=\sum_{i\notin B}a_{i}, which is a nonnegative combination of {ai}i∉B\{a_{i}\}_{i\notin B} and hence lies in cone⁡{ai:i∉B}\operatorname{cone}\{a_{i}:i\notin B\}. By conic Carathéodory (see e.g. (Bertsekas, 2009, Prop. 1.2.1(a))), every element of this cone is a positive combination of a linearly independent subfamily, so −∑b∈Bab=∑i∈Cαiai-\sum_{b\in B}a_{b}=\sum_{i\in C}\alpha_{i}a_{i} with αi>0\alpha_{i}>0, C⊆[N]∖BC\subseteq[N]\setminus B and |C|≤qB|C|\leq q_{B}. If the target is 00, take C=∅C=\varnothing. Set cb=1c_{b}=1 on BB, ci=αic_{i}=\alpha_{i} on CC, and 00 elsewhere. ∎

Remark B.2 (Effective residual dimension).

The proof used only that the residual dyads lie in ℝm⊗T\mathbb{R}^{m}\otimes T. If s=dimspan⁡{ρ1,…,ρN}s=\dim\operatorname{span}\{\rho_{1},\dots,\rho_{N}\}, they lie in the s​rsr-dimensional space span⁡{ρi}⊗T\operatorname{span}\{\rho_{i}\}\otimes T, and the same argument gives τ⁡(D)≤r+s​r=(s+1)​r\tau(D)\leq r+sr=(s+1)r for r≥1r\geq 1. Theorem 3.4 (Threshold; restated). n⋆​(d,m)=(m+1)​dn^{\star}(d,m)=(m+1)d for all d,m≥2d,m\geq 2 (and in fact for all d,m≥1d,m\geq 1, cf. Remark 2.4), and Fweighted​(d,m,n)=1F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,n)=1 for all n≥(m+1)​dn\geq(m+1)d.

Proof.

Theorem 3.1 gives ratio 11 at budget (m+1)​d(m+1)d for every dataset, and Theorem 3.3 exhibits a dataset with ratio >1>1 at budget (m+1)​d−1(m+1)d-1. The content of this section is the upper bound Fweighted​(d,m,d)≤d+1F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,d)\leq d+1 uniformly in mm, which requires selecting one subset that serves all mm output rows simultaneously.

Volume sampling.

Let X∈ℝd×NX\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N} have full row rank and let y∈ℝNy\in\mathbb{R}^{N}. Size-dd volume sampling draws a subset SS of dd column indices with probability proportional to det(XS)2\det(X_{S})^{2}. Let w⁡(S)w(S) denote the least-squares solution of the subproblem (XS,yS)(X_{S},y_{S}) (the interpolant when XSX_{S} is invertible). Dereziński and Warmuth (2017) proved two results. The first is unbiasedness: 𝔼⁡[w⁡(S)]=w⋆\mathbb{E}[w(S)]=w^{\star} for every label vector, requiring only full row rank (their Theorem 3 and Proposition 7). The second bounds the total square loss LL on the full data:

𝔼⁡[L⁡(w⁡(S))]≤(d+1)​L​(w⋆),\mathbb{E}\bigl[L(w(S))\bigr]\ \leq\ (d+1)\,L(w^{\star}), (7)

with equality when XX is in general position (every dd-column submatrix nonsingular), as stated in their Theorem 5. We only use the inequality (7), which holds without general position. Equality in (7) can fail for degenerate XX (e.g. x1=x2=e1x_{1}=x_{2}=e_{1}, x3=x4=e2x_{3}=x_{4}=e_{2}, y=(1,−1,1,−1)y=(1,-1,1,-1) has 𝔼⁡[L⁡(w⁡(S))]=2​L​(w⋆)\mathbb{E}[L(w(S))]=2L(w^{\star})). Dividing by NN converts (7) to average losses.

Proof of Theorem 6.1.

Only Fweighted​(d,m,d)≤d+1F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,d)\leq d+1 remains. Fix a dataset and let r=rankr=\operatorname{rank} of the features. If r=0r=0, the ratio is 11 because both rules return W=0W=0. If LD⋆=0L^{\star}_{D}=0, choose rr points whose features form a basis of TT with positive weights. The weighted problem then has minimum 00 and minimizer set W∘+{H:H​PT=0}W^{\circ}+\{H:HP_{T}=0\}. The Frobenius rule returns W∘W^{\circ}, so the ratio is 11 by the 0/00/0 convention.

Otherwise, choose an orthonormal basis U∈ℝd×rU\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r} of TT and write xi=U​ξix_{i}=U\xi_{i} with Ξ=[ξ1⋯ξN]∈ℝr×N\Xi=[\xi_{1}\cdots\xi_{N}]\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times N} of full row rank. 𝔼⁡[LD​(WS)]≤(r+1)​LD⋆≤(d+1)​LD⋆,\mathbb{E}\bigl[L_{D}(W_{S})\bigr]\ \leq\ (r+1)\,L^{\star}_{D}\ \leq\ (d+1)\,L^{\star}_{D},

Appendix D Proofs for Sections 4 and 5

Throughout this section, fix a dataset with residual dyads Mi=ρi​xi⊤M_{i}=\rho_{i}x_{i}^{\top} and recall the minimal certificate size τ⁡(D)\tau(D) from (3). Theorem 3.1 gives τ⁡(D)≤max⁡{1,(m+1)​r}\tau(D)\leq\max\{1,(m+1)r\}. The upper bound at budget (m+1)​d−1(m+1)d-1 requires understanding the datasets with τ⁡(D)=(m+1)​d\tau(D)=(m+1)d, which we call certificate-maximal. The key is a rigidity theorem for maximal certificates.

D.1 Rigidity of maximal certificates

Theorem 4.1 (Determinant–facet rigidity; restated). Let the features span ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and suppose τ⁡(D)=k:=(m+1)​d\tau(D)=k:=(m+1)d. Let cc be a spanning zero certificate with |supp⁡c|=k|\operatorname{supp}c|=k and support SS. Then SS splits uniquely (up to permutation) into dd pairwise disjoint blocks S=C1⊔⋯⊔CdS=C_{1}\sqcup\dots\sqcup C_{d} with |Cj|=m+1|C_{j}|=m+1, where each CjC_{j} supports a positive circuit of the dyads whose features span a one-dimensional line UjU_{j}, and U1,…,UdU_{1},\dots,U_{d} are linearly independent.

Proof.

The proof has four steps. We first identify the normalized nonnegative kernel as a polytope, then use the determinant polynomial to bound its number of facets. This shows that the polytope is a simplex. Finally, we read off line-supported circuits from the extreme rays. Vectorize the dyads into 𝖠=[vec⁡(Mi)]i∈S∈ℝm​d×k\mathsf{A}=[\mathrm{vec}(M_{i})]_{i\in S}\in\mathbb{R}^{md\times k} and let K=ker⁡𝖠∩ℝ≥0kK=\ker\mathsf{A}\cap\mathbb{R}^{k}_{\geq 0}, h=dimker⁡𝖠≥k−m​d=dh=\dim\ker\mathsf{A}\geq k-md=d. Since c>0c>0 on SS and lies in ker⁡𝖠\ker\mathsf{A}, a neighborhood of cc in ker⁡𝖠\ker\mathsf{A} remains nonnegative. Thus KK spans ker⁡𝖠\ker\mathsf{A}, and the compact section P=K∩{𝟏⊤θ=1}P=K\cap\{\mathbf{1}^{\top}\theta=1\} is a polytope of dimension h−1h-1 whose relative interior consists exactly of the strictly positive points.

Consider f⁡(θ)=det(∑i∈Sθi​xi​xi⊤)f(\theta)=\det\bigl(\sum_{i\in S}\theta_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\bigr), a polynomial of degree at most dd. On relint⁡P\operatorname{relint}P, all weights are positive and the features span ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, so f>0f>0. At any boundary point, some coordinate vanishes. If f>0f>0 there, the positively weighted features would span ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and the point would be a spanning zero certificate of support ≤k−1\leq k-1, contradicting τ=k\tau=k. Hence f≡0f\equiv 0 on every facet of PP. Parametrizing aff​P\mathrm{aff}\,P by ℝh−1\mathbb{R}^{h-1}, the restriction gg of ff is a nonzero polynomial of degree ≤d\leq d. It vanishes on the relative interior of each facet and is therefore divisible by the pairwise non-associated affine linear forms of the distinct facet hyperplanes. Thus PP has at most dd facets. If h≥2h\geq 2, then PP has positive dimension and, being bounded, at least hh facets, so h≤dh\leq d. If h=1h=1, then h≤dh\leq d trivially. Together with h≥dh\geq d, this gives h=dh=d. Thus, for d≥2d\geq 2, PP is a (d−1)(d-1)-dimensional polytope with exactly dd facets and hence a (d−1)(d-1)-simplex. For d=1d=1, PP is a single point. In both cases, KK is a simplicial cone with extreme rays v(1),…,v(d)v^{(1)},\dots,v^{(d)}.

Let Uj=span⁡{xi:vi(j)>0}U_{j}=\operatorname{span}\{x_{i}:v^{(j)}_{i}>0\}. As cc is a strictly positive combination of all rays, the supports of the rays cover SS, so ∑jUj=ℝd\sum_{j}U_{j}=\mathbb{R}^{d}. If d=1d=1, there is a single ray and U1=ℝU_{1}=\mathbb{R}, so dimU1=1\dim U_{1}=1. Now let d≥2d\geq 2. Dropping ray jj and normalizing the sum of the remaining rays gives a boundary point of PP, where the features cannot span, so ∑ℓ≠jUℓ≠ℝd\sum_{\ell\neq j}U_{\ell}\neq\mathbb{R}^{d} for each jj: the family {Uj}\{U_{j}\} is a minimal spanning family. Choose functionals ϕj\phi_{j} vanishing on ∑ℓ≠jUℓ\sum_{\ell\neq j}U_{\ell} and not on UjU_{j}, and normalize them against vectors uj∈Uju_{j}\in U_{j} with ϕj​(uj)=1\phi_{j}(u_{j})=1. Then (ϕj)(\phi_{j}) is a dual basis, and Uj⊆⋂i≠jker⁡ϕiU_{j}\subseteq\bigcap_{i\neq j}\ker\phi_{i}, a one-dimensional space, so dimUj=1\dim U_{j}=1 in every dimension d≥1d\geq 1.

Each extreme ray of the cone {θ≥0:𝖠​θ=0}\{\theta\geq 0:\mathsf{A}\theta=0\} has inclusion-minimal support CjC_{j}, and dimker⁡𝖠Cj=1\dim\ker\mathsf{A}_{C_{j}}=1. Otherwise, a two-sided perturbation along a second kernel direction would split the ray. All dyads of CjC_{j} lie in ℝm⊗Uj\mathbb{R}^{m}\otimes U_{j}, a space of dimension mm, so |Cj|=rank⁡𝖠Cj+1≤m+1|C_{j}|=\operatorname{rank}\mathsf{A}_{C_{j}}+1\leq m+1. Finally, k=|S|≤∑j|Cj|≤d⁡(m+1)=kk=|S|\leq\sum_{j}|C_{j}|\leq d(m+1)=k forces every |Cj|=m+1|C_{j}|=m+1 and pairwise disjoint supports. The decomposition is unique because the extreme rays of KK are. ∎

D.2 Certificate-maximal datasets live on dd lines

Theorem 4.1 describes one maximal certificate. We now use the maximality of τ⁡(D)\tau(D) to show that the same line-circuit structure governs every nonzero-feature point of the dataset.

Theorem 4.2 (Line structure; restated). Let the features span ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and τ⁡(D)=(m+1)​d=k\tau(D)=(m+1)d=k. Then:

  1. 1.

    every data point with xi≠0x_{i}\neq 0 belongs to some positive circuit of dyads supported on a single feature line and of size exactly m+1m+1;

  2. 2.

    there is no positive circuit of dyads whose features span a subspace of dimension ≥2\geq 2, and no line circuit of size ≤m\leq m; in particular no point has xi≠0x_{i}\neq 0 and ρi=0\rho_{i}=0;

  3. 3.

    the nonzero features lie on exactly dd linearly independent lines.

Consequently, any dataset whose nonzero features are not of this dd-line form satisfies τ⁡(D)≤(m+1)​d−1\tau(D)\leq(m+1)d-1 and is recovered exactly within budget (m+1)​d−1(m+1)d-1.

Proof.

(1) Extend xtx_{t}, with tt fixed and xt≠0x_{t}\neq 0, to a feature basis B∋tB\ni t and apply Lemma B.1: the resulting certificate has support at most kk and, since τ=k\tau=k, exactly kk. Theorem 4.1 splits it into (m+1)(m+1)-point line circuits, one of which contains tt.

(2) Let CC be a positive circuit whose features span an ss-dimensional space with s≥2s\geq 2. Then |C|≤m​s+1|C|\leq ms+1 because its dyads lie in an m​sms-dimensional space. Extend the features of CC by d−sd-s data points to a basis of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and attach to each added point its (m+1)(m+1)-point line circuit from (1). Summing all these positive relations gives a spanning zero certificate of support at most m​s+1+(d−s)​(m+1)=k−s+1≤k−1ms+1+(d-s)(m+1)=k-s+1\leq k-1, contradicting τ=k\tau=k. A line circuit of size ≤m\leq m similarly completes with d−1d-1 line circuits to support ≤m+(d−1)​(m+1)=k−1\leq m+(d-1)(m+1)=k-1. A point with xi≠0=ρix_{i}\neq 0=\rho_{i} is by itself a 11-point line “circuit” (Mi=0M_{i}=0) and is excluded the same way.

(3) Suppose d+1d+1 distinct nonzero feature lines exist. Take an (m+1)(m+1)-point line circuit on each using (1), and let JJ be their disjoint union, |J|=(d+1)​(m+1)|J|=(d+1)(m+1). Then dimker⁡𝖠J≥|J|−m​d=d+m+1\dim\ker\mathsf{A}_{J}\geq|J|-md=d+m+1. The sum of the circuits’ positive kernel vectors is strictly positive on JJ, so the nonnegative kernel cone spans ker⁡𝖠J\ker\mathsf{A}_{J}. But each extreme ray of that cone is a positive circuit, hence by (2) supported on a single line and of size m+1m+1. On each line, the kernel of the corresponding block is one-dimensional, so there are at most d+1d+1 extreme rays, spanning at most d+1d+1 dimensions. This contradicts d+m+1>d+1d+m+1>d+1. As the features span ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, there are exactly dd independent lines. ∎

D.3 The mm-point mean lemma

For a positive (m+1)(m+1)-point circuit, deleting one vertex leaves an mm-point mean. The lemma shows that some deletion moves the mean by at most a 1/m1/m fraction of the root-mean-square radius.

Lemma 5.1 (mm-point mean lemma; restated). Let zi∈ℝmz_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} carry weights pi>0p_{i}>0 with ∑ipi=1\sum_{i}p_{i}=1 and ∑ipi​zi=0\sum_{i}p_{i}z_{i}=0, and let E=∑ipi​∥zi∥2E=\sum_{i}p_{i}\lVert z_{i}\rVert^{2}. Then some convex combination δ\delta of at most mm of the points satisfies ∥δ∥2≤E/m2\lVert\delta\rVert^{2}\leq E/m^{2}. The constant is attained by the uniformly weighted regular simplex.

Proof.

By conic Carathéodory, decompose pp inside the cone {q≥0:∑iqi​zi=0}\{q\geq 0:\sum_{i}q_{i}z_{i}=0\} as a positive combination of positive circuits (extreme rays), each of support at most m+1m+1, and normalize each circuit to a probability vector q(α)q^{(\alpha)}. Thus p=∑αλα​q(α)p=\sum_{\alpha}\lambda_{\alpha}q^{(\alpha)} with λα>0\lambda_{\alpha}>0 and ∑αλα=∑ipi=1\sum_{\alpha}\lambda_{\alpha}=\sum_{i}p_{i}=1. The second moments Eq(α)E_{q^{(\alpha)}} then average to EE, so some circuit qq has Eq≤EE_{q}\leq E. If Eq=0E_{q}=0, all its points vanish and a single point gives δ=0\delta=0. If its support has size ≤m\leq m, its own zero mean is the desired δ=0\delta=0. Otherwise, the support has weights q1,…,qm+1>0q_{1},\dots,q_{m+1}>0 with ∑jqj​zj=0\sum_{j}q_{j}z_{j}=0. Deleting point jj leaves the convex combination μj=−qj1−qj​zj\mu_{j}=-\frac{q_{j}}{1-q_{j}}z_{j} of the other mm points. With tj=qj​∥zj∥2/Eqt_{j}=q_{j}\lVert z_{j}\rVert^{2}/E_{q} (so ∑jtj=1\sum_{j}t_{j}=1), ∥μj∥2/Eq=qj​tj/(1−qj)2\lVert\mu_{j}\rVert^{2}/E_{q}=q_{j}t_{j}/(1-q_{j})^{2}. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives ∑j(1−qj)2qj=∑j1qj−2​(m+1)+1≥(m+1)2−2​(m+1)+1=m2\sum_{j}\frac{(1-q_{j})^{2}}{q_{j}}=\sum_{j}\frac{1}{q_{j}}-2(m+1)+1\geq(m+1)^{2}-2(m+1)+1=m^{2}. Hence not all jj can violate ∥μj∥2≤Eq/m2\lVert\mu_{j}\rVert^{2}\leq E_{q}/m^{2}, for otherwise summing tj>(1−qj)2m2​qjt_{j}>\frac{(1-q_{j})^{2}}{m^{2}q_{j}} over jj yields 1>11>1. Finally, Eq≤EE_{q}\leq E. For tightness, consider the uniformly weighted regular simplex with vertices r1,…,rm+1r_{1},\dots,r_{m+1}, so E=∥rj∥2E=\lVert r_{j}\rVert^{2} for every jj. Every set of at most mm vertices lies in a facet. The point of the facet opposite rjr_{j} closest to the origin is its centroid −rj/m-r_{j}/m, and ∥rj/m∥2=E/m2\lVert r_{j}/m\rVert^{2}=E/m^{2}. Hence no convex combination of at most mm vertices has smaller squared norm, and the deletions μj\mu_{j} attain it. ∎

D.4 Assembly

The budget deficit is exactly one point. We therefore fit all but one feature line exactly and spend only mm points on the line with the smallest residual energy.

Theorem 5.2 (Near-threshold value; restated). For all d,m≥2d,m\geq 2 (and in fact for all d,m≥1d,m\geq 1, cf. Remark 2.4), Fweighted​(d,m,(m+1)​d−1)=1+1d​m2F_{\mathrm{weighted}}\bigl(d,m,(m+1)d-1\bigr)=1+\dfrac{1}{dm^{2}}.

If the feature rank is r<dr<d, Theorem 3.1 gives a certificate of support at most max⁡{1,(m+1)​r}≤n0\max\{1,(m+1)r\}\leq n_{0}, with one point when r=0r=0, and the ratio is 11. The same holds if LD⋆=0L^{\star}_{D}=0, by basis selection as in Section 6.1, or if τ⁡(D)≤n0\tau(D)\leq n_{0}. In the remaining certificate-maximal case τ⁡(D)=(m+1)​d\tau(D)=(m+1)d, Theorem 4.2 provides a basis u1,…,udu_{1},\dots,u_{d} and scalars si≠0s_{i}\neq 0 with xi=si​uj⁡(i)x_{i}=s_{i}u_{j(i)} for every nonzero-feature point. Reading the first-order condition ∑iMi=0\sum_{i}M_{i}=0 against the basis (uj)(u_{j}), each line satisfies ∑i∈Ijsi​ρi=0\sum_{i\in I_{j}}s_{i}\rho_{i}=0. Set, per line,

zi=ρi/si,pi=si2/gj,gj=∑i∈Ijsi2,Rj=∑i∈Ij∥ρi∥2,z_{i}=\rho_{i}/s_{i},\qquad p_{i}=s_{i}^{2}/g_{j},\qquad g_{j}=\sum_{i\in I_{j}}s_{i}^{2},\qquad R_{j}=\sum_{i\in I_{j}}\lVert\rho_{i}\rVert^{2},

so that ∑i∈Ijpi​zi=0\sum_{i\in I_{j}}p_{i}z_{i}=0 and ∑ipi​∥zi∥2=Rj/gj\sum_{i}p_{i}\lVert z_{i}\rVert^{2}=R_{j}/g_{j}. Choose the lightest line j⋆j_{\star} with Rj⋆≤1d​∑jRj≤N​LD⋆dR_{j_{\star}}\leq\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j}R_{j}\leq\frac{NL^{\star}_{D}}{d} (features equal to 00 only increase LD⋆L^{\star}_{D}). On each line j≠j⋆j\neq j_{\star}, the probability vector (pi)i∈Ij(p_{i})_{i\in I_{j}} is a nonzero element of the pointed cone {θ≥0:∑i∈Ijθi​zi=0}\{\theta\geq 0:\sum_{i\in I_{j}}\theta_{i}z_{i}=0\}. Decompose it into extreme rays, take one of them, and normalize it to coordinate sum one. This gives a positive zero-mean combination of the ziz_{i} supported on a positive circuit, hence on at most m+1m+1 points (Definition 2.3). On line j⋆j_{\star} pick at most mm points and a convex combination δ\delta with ∥δ∥2≤Rj⋆m2​gj⋆\lVert\delta\rVert^{2}\leq\frac{R_{j_{\star}}}{m^{2}g_{j_{\star}}} (Lemma 5.1). Translate the per-line convex coefficients αi\alpha_{i} into selection weights ci=αi/si2>0c_{i}=\alpha_{i}/s_{i}^{2}>0, rescaling each line independently and normalizing globally. The weighted normal equations then decouple along the basis and give W^=W∘+H\widehat{W}=W^{\circ}+H with H​uj=0Hu_{j}=0 for j≠j⋆j\neq j_{\star} and H​uj⋆=−δHu_{j_{\star}}=-\delta. The selected features contain all dd lines, so the weighted Gram matrix is positive definite and the minimizer is unique. The support has size at most (d−1)​(m+1)+m=n0(d-1)(m+1)+m=n_{0}. Pad the selection by Lemma 2.1 if fewer slots are used. By (5),

LD​(W^)−LD⋆=gj⋆​∥δ∥2N≤Rj⋆N​m2≤LD⋆d​m2.L_{D}(\widehat{W})-L^{\star}_{D}=\frac{g_{j_{\star}}\lVert\delta\rVert^{2}}{N}\leq\frac{R_{j_{\star}}}{Nm^{2}}\leq\frac{L^{\star}_{D}}{dm^{2}}.

Take the regular-simplex axial instance: let r1,…,rm+1∈ℝmr_{1},\dots,r_{m+1}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} be regular simplex vertices with ∑jrj=0\sum_{j}r_{j}=0 and ∥rj∥2=mm+1\lVert r_{j}\rVert^{2}=\frac{m}{m+1}, whose facets are at squared distance h2=1m⁡(m+1)h^{2}=\frac{1}{m(m+1)} from the origin. For any selection of support at most N−1N-1, some axis is either empty, in which case the Frobenius rule sets its column to zero with deviation ∥w∥2=h2\lVert w\rVert^{2}=h^{2}, or represented by a proper subset, with deviation at least the facet distance h2h^{2}. By the analogue of (6), the loss exceeds LD⋆L^{\star}_{D} by at least h2/dh^{2}/d, and deleting one vertex with uniform facet weights attains it. The ratio is 1+h2/dm/(m+1)=1+1d​m21+\frac{h^{2}/d}{m/(m+1)}=1+\frac{1}{dm^{2}}. ∎

Remark D.1 (General centered-simplex families).

The same computation applies to any centered simplex r1,…,rm+1r_{1},\dots,r_{m+1} (∑jrj=0\sum_{j}r_{j}=0, S=∑j∥rj∥2S=\sum_{j}\lVert r_{j}\rVert^{2}, h=minj⁡dist⁡(0,conv⁡{rk}k≠j)h=\min_{j}\operatorname{dist}(0,\operatorname{conv}\{r_{k}\}_{k\neq j})), provided the columns of W∘W^{\circ} are chosen with ∥W∘​ei∥≥h\lVert W^{\circ}e_{i}\rVert\geq h: the exact (N−1)(N-1)-point ratio is 1+(m+1)​h2d​S1+\frac{(m+1)h^{2}}{dS}. Within this family, h2≤S/(m2​(m+1))h^{2}\leq S/(m^{2}(m+1)) with equality exactly for regular simplices. Indeed, the centroid of the facet opposite rjr_{j} is −rj/m-r_{j}/m, so h2≤minj⁡∥rj∥2/m2≤S/(m2​(m+1))h^{2}\leq\min_{j}\lVert r_{j}\rVert^{2}/m^{2}\leq S/(m^{2}(m+1)). Equality forces all ∥rj∥\lVert r_{j}\rVert to be equal and each facet centroid to be the point of that facet nearest the origin, i.e. ⟨rj,rk⟩\langle r_{j},r_{k}\rangle independent of k≠jk\neq j. Thus, in the equality case, all pairwise inner products coincide and the simplex is regular. For m≥2m\geq 2, the integer instance of Definition 3.2 realizes the slightly smaller rational value of Theorem 3.3 with integer data. For m=1m=1, the two values coincide.

Appendix E The complex dictionary and proofs for Section 6.2

For d,m≥2d,m\geq 2 and d<n<(m+1)​d−1d<n<(m+1)d-1, the profile Fweighted​(d,m,n)F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(d,m,n) remains open. For d=1d=1, it is given by Corollary G.3. The corresponding scalar regime also remains open, apart from the cells settled in (Zhang, 2026): it is the intermediate regime of Question 2 of (Hanneke et al., 2025b). In this section we treat the smallest cell (d,m)=(2,2)(d,m)=(2,2), where the open budgets are n=3,4n=3,4. We prove the interval theorem (Theorem 6.4) and reduce the conjectured exact values to a finite moment problem. The evidence for the conjecture is collected in Appendix F.

Hence the infimum is at most ∥βi∥2=12​|zi|2≤E2\lVert\beta_{i}\rVert^{2}=\frac{1}{2}|z_{i}|^{2}\leq\frac{E}{2}. ∎

E.5 The interval theorem

Theorem 6.4 (restated). Fweighted​(2,2,3)∈[138,158]F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(2,2,3)\in\bigl[\frac{13}{8},\frac{15}{8}\bigr] and Fweighted​(2,2,4)∈[54,32]F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(2,2,4)\in\bigl[\frac{5}{4},\frac{3}{2}\bigr].

The lower bounds follow from Proposition 6.3. For the upper bounds, fix a dataset and a budget n∈{3,4}n\in\{3,4\}. If the feature rank is r≤1r\leq 1, then τ⁡(D)≤max⁡{1,(m+1)​r}≤3≤n\tau(D)\leq\max\{1,(m+1)r\}\leq 3\leq n (Theorem 3.1; one point when r=0r=0) and the ratio is 11. The ratio is also one if LD⋆=0L^{\star}_{D}=0 or τ⁡(D)≤n\tau(D)\leq n. Otherwise, the dictionary of Appendix E.2 applies, and by (9) and Lemma E.5 (a three-point selection is also a four-point selection) the ratio is at most 1+Γ3≤1581+\Gamma_{3}\leq\frac{15}{8} for n=3n=3 and at most 1+Γ4≤321+\Gamma_{4}\leq\frac{3}{2} for n=4n=4. The closure points used in Lemmas E.4–E.5 are limits of admissible selections within the same budget. This suffices because the inner optimization in FweightedF_{\mathrm{weighted}} is an infimum. ∎

E.6 The conjecture

Conjecture 6.5 (restated). Fweighted​(2,2,3)=138F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(2,2,3)=\frac{13}{8} and Fweighted​(2,2,4)=54F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(2,2,4)=\frac{5}{4}. Equivalently, for every moment system,

inf|supp⁡q|≤3,|μ|<1C⁡(q)≤5​E8andinf|supp⁡q|≤4,|μ|<1C⁡(q)≤E4.\inf_{|\operatorname{supp}q|\leq 3,\ |\mu|<1}C(q)\leq\frac{5E}{8}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\inf_{|\operatorname{supp}q|\leq 4,\ |\mu|<1}C(q)\leq\frac{E}{4}.
Remark E.6 (The two formulations are equivalent).

The moment inequalities imply the equalities by the branch analysis in the proof of Theorem 6.4 together with the lower bounds of Proposition 6.3. Conversely, suppose a moment system violates one of the inequalities, say inf|supp⁡q|≤kC⁡(q)=v​E\inf_{|\operatorname{supp}q|\leq k}C(q)=vE with v>cv>c. Realize it as a whitened dataset (xi,ρi)(x_{i},\rho_{i}) as in Appendix E.2 and add a large linear signal: yi=L​U​xi−ρiy_{i}=L\,Ux_{i}-\rho_{i} with UU invertible, so that W∘=L​UW^{\circ}=LU and the residuals are the given ρi\rho_{i}. For a non-spanning selection with feature span PSP_{S}, the minimum-Frobenius-norm solution is L​U​PS+RS​PSLUP_{S}+R_{S}P_{S}, whose deviation from the full minimizer L​ULU has squared Frobenius norm L2​∥U⁡(I−PS)∥F2+∥RS​PS∥F2≥L2​∥U⁡(I−PS)∥F2L^{2}\lVert U(I-P_{S})\rVert_{F}^{2}+\lVert R_{S}P_{S}\rVert_{F}^{2}\geq L^{2}\lVert U(I-P_{S})\rVert_{F}^{2} because the two terms act on orthogonal feature subspaces. There are finitely many non-spanning supports, and UU is invertible, so minS⁡∥U⁡(I−PS)∥F2>0\min_{S}\lVert U(I-P_{S})\rVert_{F}^{2}>0 over these supports. For LL large, every non-spanning selection therefore has ratio above 1+v1+v as well. Thus Fweighted​(2,2,n)≥RD​(n)≥1+v>1+cF_{\mathrm{weighted}}(2,2,n)\geq R_{D}(n)\geq 1+v>1+c with c∈{58,14}c\in\{\tfrac{5}{8},\tfrac{1}{4}\}, contradicting the conjectured equalities.

E.7 Instance values versus profile values at (2,2)(2,2)

Appendix F Evidence for Conjecture 6.5: full statements and proofs

This section records five independent pieces of structural evidence for Conjecture 6.5: a finite reduction, the sharp solution of the two-direction class, a stability statement for its equality fiber, two obstructions that rule out natural proof strategies, and the classes on which the conjecture is already proved.

F.1 Finite reduction: at most seven atoms

Proposition 6.6 (restated). For fixed atoms (ti,zi)(t_{i},z_{i}), the closed set 𝒫={p∈ℝ≥0N:∑ipi=1,𝔼pt=𝔼pz=𝔼p(t¯z)=0}\mathcal{P}=\{p\in\mathbb{R}^{N}_{\geq 0}:\sum_{i}p_{i}=1,\ \mathbb{E}_{p}t=\mathbb{E}_{p}z=\mathbb{E}_{p}(\bar{t}z)=0\} is a polytope cut out by at most 77 linear equalities, whose points with full support are the admissible weight vectors. Minimizing the linear functional E⁡(p)E(p) over this polytope yields a basic feasible solution p⋆p^{\star} of support at most 77 with E⁡(p⋆)≤E⁡(p)E(p^{\star})\leq E(p). The subsystem on supp⁡p⋆\operatorname{supp}p^{\star} is again a moment system, and every selection admissible for it is admissible for the original system. Consequently each inequality of Conjecture 6.5 holds for all finite systems if and only if it holds for all systems with at most seven atoms. Since atoms may be split into identically placed copies without changing the problem, it suffices to treat systems with exactly seven labelled atoms.

Proof.

E⁡(p)E(p) is linear in pp, subject to normalization (11 equation) and the three complex moment constraints (66 real equations). A basic optimal solution has support at most the constraint rank ≤7\leq 7. Its subsystem inherits the moment conditions, and its witness lifts verbatim to the original system. If the minimum is E⋆=0E^{\star}=0, all its supported ziz_{i} vanish. In this case, 𝔼​t=0\mathbb{E}t=0 guarantees two distinct directions, and choosing one atom from each gives a two-point selection with C=0C=0. Splitting an atom (pi,ti,zi)(p_{i},t_{i},z_{i}) into (θ​pi,ti,zi),((1−θ)​pi,ti,zi)(\theta p_{i},t_{i},z_{i}),((1-\theta)p_{i},t_{i},z_{i}) changes no moments. Merging the copies in a witness does not increase its support. The number seven cannot be lowered by this route: for the seventh-roots system of Proposition F.3 the seven real constraints prescribe the Fourier coefficients of pp at frequencies 0,1,2,30,1,2,3 and hence, since pp is real, at all frequencies. Thus p=17​𝟏p=\frac{1}{7}\mathbf{1} is the only feasible weight vector. ∎

F.5 Closed classes, a necessary condition, and records

Proposition 6.7 (Classes on which Conjecture 6.5 holds; restated). The three-point inequality of Conjecture 6.5 holds for all moment systems with at most four atoms, and the four-point inequality for all systems with at most five atoms. Both inequalities hold for all two-direction systems, and the four-point inequality holds for all antipodally paired systems (disjoint unions of pairs {(t,z),(−t,z)}\{(t,z),(-t,z)\} with equal zz-values inside each pair).

Proof.

Systems with fewer atoms than the budget are trivial: q=pq=p gives C=0C=0. If E=0E=0, then every zi=0z_{i}=0. In this zero-energy case, 𝔼p​t=0\mathbb{E}_{p}t=0 ensures that at least two distinct directions occur, and choosing one atom from each of two such directions gives |μ|<1|\mu|<1 and ν=λ=0\nu=\lambda=0, hence C=0C=0. We may therefore assume E>0E>0. If some atom has pi≥12p_{i}\geq\frac{1}{2}, then 𝔼p​t=0\mathbb{E}_{p}t=0 forces pi=12p_{i}=\frac{1}{2} and all other atoms antipodal to tit_{i}, so the system is two-directional and Proposition F.1 applies. Otherwise every pi<12p_{i}<\frac{1}{2}, and deleting a single atom ii and renormalizing the original weights on the others gives an admissible selection, since |μ|=pi/(1−pi)<1|\mu|=p_{i}/(1-p_{i})<1. Realize the system by a whitened dataset without zero-feature points and with ∑i|ξi|2=1\sum_{i}|\xi_{i}|^{2}=1, so that ∑ixi​xi⊤=12​I2\sum_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}=\frac{1}{2}I_{2} (Appendix E.2). By Lemma E.4, any counterexample to the three-point inequality must satisfy 5​|zi|2−2​Li>3​E5|z_{i}|^{2}-2L_{i}>3E for every atom ii (for pairwise distinct directions: |zi|2>3​E5|z_{i}|^{2}>\frac{3E}{5} for all ii). Appendix G The general kk-point mean lemma

Lemma 5.1 is the case k=Mk=M of a sharp family of sparsification bounds. We record this family both for its own interest and for its applications: it supplies the sharp per-line constants for the allocation problems mentioned in Section 7 and settles the whole profile for d=1d=1 (Corollary G.3). The proof is elementary and self-contained. None of Theorems 3.4, 6.1, 5.2 or 6.4 depends on this appendix. The only case used elsewhere is k=Mk=M (Lemma 5.1). In the boundary variance fact and in Sublemma G below, nn denotes the dimension of a simplex. In Corollary G.3, it again denotes the budget.

Relation to other sparsification bounds.

For k=2k=2 and M≥3M\geq 3, the constant M−12​M\frac{M-1}{2M} of Theorem G.1 coincides with, and follows from, the bound in Theorem 2 of (Dewasurendra, 2026b) after the circuit reduction used below. The cited theorem gives an equal-weight two-point bound for zero-mean distributions on at most ss atoms, with constant max⁡{13,s−22​(s−1)}\max\{\frac{1}{3},\frac{s-2}{2(s-1)}\}. The reduction restricts the circuit support to s≤M+1s\leq M+1. For M=2M=2, Lemma 5.1 gives 14\frac{1}{4} for arbitrary convex weights on two points. This feasible set differs from the equal-weight pairs behind the constant 13\frac{1}{3} in the cited result, which also does not cover general kk. A radius-normalized, equal-weight analogue concerns the worst squared distance from a point of a simplex in the unit ball to a kk-fold barycenter of its vertices. This is the sharp approximate Carathéodory theorem of (Tinarrage, 2026). That statement normalizes by the radius of a ball containing the simplex and uses equal weights, whereas Theorem G.1 normalizes by the variance EE and allows arbitrary convex weights. Thus neither is a formal special case of the other. Theorem G.1 does imply a skeleton-distance statement with radius normalization and a weaker, face-distance conclusion. If the vertices viv_{i} of an MM-simplex lie in the unit ball and y=∑iqi​viy=\sum_{i}q_{i}v_{i} with qi>0q_{i}>0, then E=∑iqi​∥vi−y∥2=∑iqi​∥vi∥2−∥y∥2≤1−∥y∥2E=\sum_{i}q_{i}\lVert v_{i}-y\rVert^{2}=\sum_{i}q_{i}\lVert v_{i}\rVert^{2}-\lVert y\rVert^{2}\leq 1-\lVert y\rVert^{2}, so some face FF spanned by at most kk vertices satisfies dist⁡(y,F)2≤M+1−kk​M​(1−∥y∥2)\operatorname{dist}(y,F)^{2}\leq\frac{M+1-k}{kM}\,(1-\lVert y\rVert^{2}).

Theorem G.1 (kk-point mean lemma).

Let M≥1M\geq 1 and let zi∈ℝMz_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{M} carry weights pi>0p_{i}>0, ∑ipi=1\sum_{i}p_{i}=1, with ∑ipi​zi=0\sum_{i}p_{i}z_{i}=0, and E=∑ipi​∥zi∥2E=\sum_{i}p_{i}\lVert z_{i}\rVert^{2}. For every 1≤k≤M+11\leq k\leq M+1 there is a convex combination δ\delta of at most kk of the points with

∥δ∥2≤E⋅M+1−kk​M.\lVert\delta\rVert^{2}\ \leq\ E\cdot\frac{M+1-k}{kM}.

The constant is sharp: for the uniformly weighted regular MM-simplex, every convex combination supported on kk points has squared norm at least E​M+1−kk​ME\frac{M+1-k}{kM}, with equality for kk vertices at equal weights.

The proof has two steps: (i) reduce to a single positive circuit of support s≤M+1s\leq M+1 (extreme points of the zero-mean polytope, as in Lemma 5.1); (ii) apply the following sparsification lemma with ai=zia_{i}=z_{i}.

Lemma G.2 (Simplex skeleton sparsification).

Let s≥2s\geq 2, let a1,…,asa_{1},\dots,a_{s} lie in a Hilbert space, let qq be a probability vector with full support ss, and let Vq=∑iqi​∥ai−a¯q∥2V_{q}=\sum_{i}q_{i}\lVert a_{i}-\bar{a}_{q}\rVert^{2} where a¯q=∑iqi​ai\bar{a}_{q}=\sum_{i}q_{i}a_{i}. For every 1≤k≤s1\leq k\leq s there is a probability vector λ\lambda with |supp⁡λ|≤k|\operatorname{supp}\lambda|\leq k and

∥∑iλiai−a¯q∥2≤s−kk⁡(s−1)Vq.\Bigl\lVert\,\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}a_{i}-\bar{a}_{q}\Bigr\rVert^{2}\ \leq\ \frac{s-k}{k(s-1)}\,V_{q}.
Proof (the two nontrivial steps are stated in full).

We construct a martingale of probability vectors that successively eliminates coordinates. The key step is the following fact.

Boundary variance fact. Let qq have r≥2r\geq 2 positive coordinates and let H⪰0H\succeq 0 be a quadratic form. Then there is a random probability vector QHQ_{H} supported on the boundary ∂Δr={u∈Δr:mini⁡ui=0}\partial\Delta_{r}=\{u\in\Delta_{r}:\min_{i}u_{i}=0\} with 𝔼⁡[QH]=q\mathbb{E}[Q_{H}]=q and

𝔼⁡[(QH−q)⊤​H​(QH−q)]≤tr⁡(H⁡(Diag⁡q−q​q⊤))(r−1)2.\mathbb{E}\bigl[(Q_{H}-q)^{\top}H(Q_{H}-q)\bigr]\ \leq\ \frac{\operatorname{tr}\bigl(H(\operatorname{Diag}q-qq^{\top})\bigr)}{(r-1)^{2}}.

(One boundary variable per form HH suffices for our purposes.)

Proof of the fact. The left-hand side, minimized over admissible laws, is a finite moment problem on the compact set ∂Δr\partial\Delta_{r}. An optimal law with finite support exists. Strong duality gives

ΦH(q)=sup{ℓ(q):ℓaffine,ℓ(u)≤(u−q)⊤H(u−q)∀u∈∂Δr},\Phi_{H}(q)=\sup\Bigl\{\ell(q):\ \ell\ \text{affine},\ \ell(u)\leq(u-q)^{\top}H(u-q)\ \forall u\in\partial\Delta_{r}\Bigr\},

because the set of achievable pairs (mean, cost) is compact and convex and qq is a relative interior point of Δr\Delta_{r}, so the supporting hyperplane of that set at the optimal value is non-vertical. Fix a feasible ℓ\ell and write a=ℓ⁡(q)a=\ell(q). If a≤0a\leq 0, the desired bound (r−1)2​a≤tr⁡(H⁡(Diag⁡q−q​q⊤))(r-1)^{2}a\leq\operatorname{tr}(H(\operatorname{Diag}q-qq^{\top})) holds because the right-hand side is nonnegative. Otherwise, replace HH on the tangent space T={𝟏⊤y=0}T=\{\mathbf{1}^{\top}y=0\} by Hε=H+ε​PTH_{\varepsilon}=H+\varepsilon P_{T}, which is positive definite on TT and keeps ℓ\ell feasible. In this positive-value case, the bound for HεH_{\varepsilon} implies the bound for HH as ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow 0. We may therefore assume H≻0H\succ 0 on TT. Writing ℓ⁡(q+y)=a+2​⟨c,y⟩H\ell(q+y)=a+2\langle c,y\rangle_{H} (c∈Tc\in T) and R2=a+∥c∥H2>0R^{2}=a+\lVert c\rVert_{H}^{2}>0, feasibility says that the open HH-ball BH​(c,R)⊆TB_{H}(c,R)\subseteq T misses ∂Δr−q\partial\Delta_{r}-q. This ball contains 00 (as a>0a>0), a relative interior point of the convex set Δr−q\Delta_{r}-q. Since the ball is connected, BH​(c,R)⊆Δr−qB_{H}(c,R)\subseteq\Delta_{r}-q. The desired bound (r−1)2​ℓ​(q)≤tr⁡(H⁡(Diag⁡q−q​q⊤))=∑iqi​(ei−q)⊤​H​(ei−q)(r-1)^{2}\ell(q)\leq\operatorname{tr}(H(\operatorname{Diag}q-qq^{\top}))=\sum_{i}q_{i}(e_{i}-q)^{\top}H(e_{i}-q) then follows by applying the sublemma below in the Euclidean structure ⟨⋅,⋅⟩H\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{H} on TT, with n=r−1n=r-1, the simplex Δr−q\Delta_{r}-q, the ball BH​(c,R)B_{H}(c,R), and the barycentric representation 0=∑iqi​(ei−q)0=\sum_{i}q_{i}(e_{i}-q).

Sublemma G (simplex–ball interpolation). Let n≥1n\geq 1, let an nn-simplex T⊂ℝnT\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} contain the ball B⁡(c,R)B(c,R), assume ∥c∥<R\lVert c\rVert<R, and let 0=∑iqi​vi0=\sum_{i}q_{i}v_{i} be the barycentric representation of the origin in the vertices viv_{i} of TT. Then

∑iqi​∥vi∥2≥n2​(R2−∥c∥2).\sum_{i}q_{i}\lVert v_{i}\rVert^{2}\ \geq\ n^{2}\,(R^{2}-\lVert c\rVert^{2}).

n2=|∑ipi​⟨Vi−y,bi⟩|2≤(∑iqi​∥Vi−y∥2)​(∑ipi2qi​∥bi∥2)≤𝒱T​(y)​∑ipi1−ti.n^{2}=\Bigl|\sum_{i}p_{i}\langle V_{i}-y,b_{i}\rangle\Bigr|^{2}\leq\Bigl(\sum_{i}q_{i}\lVert V_{i}-y\rVert^{2}\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{i}\frac{p_{i}^{2}}{q_{i}}\lVert b_{i}\rVert^{2}\Bigr)\leq\mathcal{V}_{T}(y)\sum_{i}\frac{p_{i}}{1-t_{i}}.

The argument above does not use this inequality.)

Now iterate: starting from qq with support ss, apply the fact with H=𝖠⊤​𝖠H=\mathsf{A}^{\top}\mathsf{A} (where 𝖠=[a1⋯as]\mathsf{A}=[a_{1}\cdots a_{s}]), obtaining a boundary law QQ with 𝔼⁡[a¯Q]=a¯q\mathbb{E}[\bar{a}_{Q}]=\bar{a}_{q} and 𝔼​∥a¯Q−a¯q∥2≤Vq/(r−1)2\mathbb{E}\lVert\bar{a}_{Q}-\bar{a}_{q}\rVert^{2}\leq V_{q}/(r-1)^{2}. Proof of Theorem G.1.

Reduce to a circuit qq of support s≤M+1s\leq M+1 and second moment Eq≤EE_{q}\leq E exactly as in Lemma 5.1, handling the degenerate branches Eq=0E_{q}=0 and s≤ks\leq k as in that argument. In the remaining case, s>k≥1s>k\geq 1, so s≥2s\geq 2. Apply Lemma G.2 with ai=zia_{i}=z_{i}, a¯q=0\bar{a}_{q}=0: some kk-sparse convex δ\delta has ∥δ∥2≤s−kk⁡(s−1)​Eq\lVert\delta\rVert^{2}\leq\frac{s-k}{k(s-1)}E_{q}. Since s↦s−ks−1s\mapsto\frac{s-k}{s-1} is nondecreasing for k≥1k\geq 1, the constant is at most M+1−kk​M\frac{M+1-k}{kM}. To prove sharpness, note that for regular simplex vertices, ∥∑iαi​vi∥2=R2​(M+1M​∑iαi2−1M)≥R2​M+1−kk​M\lVert\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}v_{i}\rVert^{2}=R^{2}\bigl(\tfrac{M+1}{M}\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}^{2}-\tfrac{1}{M}\bigr)\geq R^{2}\tfrac{M+1-k}{kM} whenever |supp⁡α|≤k|\operatorname{supp}\alpha|\leq k, using ∑αi2≥1/k\sum\alpha_{i}^{2}\geq 1/k. ∎

Corollary G.3 (The full profile for d=1d=1).

For all m≥1m\geq 1 and n≥1n\geq 1,

Fweighted​(1,m,n)=1+m+1−nm​n(1≤n≤m+1),Fweighted​(1,m,n)=1(n≥m+1).F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(1,m,n)=1+\frac{m+1-n}{mn}\ \ (1\leq n\leq m+1),\qquad F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(1,m,n)=1\ \ (n\geq m+1).

Proof.

Upper bound. Fix a dataset with d=1d=1. If all xi=0x_{i}=0 the ratio is 11 (both rules return W=0W=0). Otherwise, let I={i:xi≠0}I=\{i:x_{i}\neq 0\}, g=∑i∈Ixi2g=\sum_{i\in I}x_{i}^{2}, pi=xi2/gp_{i}=x_{i}^{2}/g, ai=yi/xi∈ℝma_{i}=y_{i}/x_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and μ=∑i∈Ipi​ai\mu=\sum_{i\in I}p_{i}a_{i}. The full-data minimizer is the column W∘=μW^{\circ}=\mu. With E=∑i∈Ipi​∥ai−μ∥2E=\sum_{i\in I}p_{i}\lVert a_{i}-\mu\rVert^{2}, we have g​E≤N​LD⋆gE\leq NL^{\star}_{D} (the difference is the loss on zero-feature points). The selection weights ci∝αi/xi2c_{i}\propto\alpha_{i}/x_{i}^{2} have the unique minimizer W^=∑iαi​ai\widehat{W}=\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}a_{i}. By (5), the excess loss is g​∥W^−μ∥2/N≤LD⋆​m+1−nm​ng\lVert\widehat{W}-\mu\rVert^{2}/N\leq L^{\star}_{D}\frac{m+1-n}{mn}. Lower bound.
